beats.script_body: For many years, Greenwich Village was the center of New York City's lesbian and gay community, and it remains the focus of legend and history. A walk through its streets passes landmarks from more than one hundred years of the lesbian and gay past. The Village is also home to the movement's most sacred site: the building that once housed the Stonewall Inn, where three days of unrest in June 1969 are widely considered the spark that launched the modern lesbian-and-gay liberation movement.
key_claims: Greenwich Village was for many years the center of NYC's lesbian and gay community
The Village contains landmarks from over 100 years of lesbian and gay history
The Stonewall Inn building is the movement's most sacred site
Three days of unrest in June 1969 launched the modern liberation movement
beats.source_passage: While the geographic center of gay and lesbian life in the city has been shifting in recent years (for men, up to Chelsea, and for women, out to Brooklyn), Greenwich Village remains the focus of legend and history, and a walk through the streets of the Village will take you past landmarks from more than one hundred years of the lesbian and gay past. Greenwich Village is also home to the gay-and-lesbian rights movement's most sacred site: the building that once housed the Stonewall Inn, site of the legendary Stonewall riots. The three days of unrest that took place there in June 1969 are widely considered the spark that launched the modern lesbian-and-gay liberation movement.

beats.script_body: With its mix of immigrant, elite, and artistic populations, the Village was a refuge for lesbians and gay men for nearly a century before the Stonewall riots. They prized the anonymity and freedom of its streets, tenements, and boarding houses, and the relative openness of its bohemian society. Once the subway was extended down Seventh Avenue South, the Village became accessible from all parts of the city and gained a reputation as 'the place where the Bronx meets Brooklyn' for a taste of wild nightlife.
key_claims: The Village was a refuge for lesbians and gay men for nearly a century before the riots
Patrons prized the anonymity and freedom of its streets and boarding houses
Once the subway reached Seventh Avenue South it became known as 'where the Bronx meets Brooklyn'
beats.source_passage: With its mix of immigrant, elite, and artistic populations, the Village was a refuge for lesbians and gay men from all walks of life for nearly a century before the riots. They prized the anonymity and freedom of its streets, tenements, and boarding houses and the relative openness of its bohemian society. Once the subway was extended down Seventh Avenue South, the Village was accessible from all parts of the city and became known as "the place where the Bronx meets Brooklyn" for a taste of wild nightlife.

beats.script_body: The earliest evidence of gay life in New York is also the most macabre: criminal statutes against 'sodomy,' which in New York and New Amsterdam was narrowly defined as sex between men. In 1613, under Dutch rule, such activity was punishable by death, and it remained among New York's eleven capital crimes after the English duke of York established his laws in 1665. The executions were gruesome. On June 25, 1646, a black man named Jan Creoli was sentenced to be 'choked to death and then burnt to ashes,' and on June 17, 1660, Jan Quisthout pleaded guilty to the same charge and was condemned to be 'tied in a sack and cast into the river and drowned until dead.'
key_claims: In New York and New Amsterdam sodomy was defined as sex between men
In 1613 under Dutch rule it was punishable by death
It remained among New York's eleven capital crimes after 1665
Jan Creoli was sentenced June 25, 1646 to be choked and burnt to ashes
Jan Quisthout on June 17, 1660 was condemned to be sacked and drowned
beats.source_passage: In New York and New Amsterdam, sodomy was narrowly defined to cover only sex between men. In 1613, when the Dutch established their rule over New Amsterdam, sexual activity between men was punishable by death. In 1665, when the English duke of York established his laws for the colony, sodomy remained among New York's eleven capital crimes. Executions for sodomy in New York City were gruesome: on June 25, 1646, a black man named Jan Creoli was sentenced to be "choked to death and then burnt to ashes" for having sex with another man, and on June 17, 1660, Jan Quisthout pleaded guilty to the same charge and was condemned to be "tied in a sack and cast into the river and drowned until dead."

beats.script_body: By the late 1800s, New Yorkers were well aware of gay men and lesbians in their midst. In 1889 the American Observer wrote that 'there is in every community of any size a colony of male sexual perverts who are usually known to each other and are likely to congregate together.' In Greenwich Village at the time, clubs featuring waiters in drag had become a top tourist attraction.

beats.script_body: Lesbian lives were far less visible on the streets, but awareness of women's relationships grew in certain circles. Temperance leader Frances Willard, who herself had several romances with other women, observed in the late nineteenth century: 'The loves of women for each other grow more numerous each day. That so little is said about them surprises me, for they are everywhere.'

beats.source_passage: In the late nineteenth century, relationships between women were common within communities of educated women of some financial means. Temperance leader Frances Willard, who herself had several romances with other women, observed, "The loves of women for each other grow more numerous each day. That so little is said about them surprises me, for they are everywhere."

beats.script_body: This intersection is famously confusing. With your back to the newsstand atop the uptown 1/9 subway stop, look for the very tall brick building with a bas-relief of a seahorse just above the ground-floor door facing you. That's Sheridan Square — the street, not the square itself. Keep the seahorse building on your left and you're heading the right way.

beats.script_body: Café Society, an integrated club known as 'the wrong place for the right people,' filled the basement of the two buildings — one is 1 Sheridan Square — that meet where Barrow Street and Washington Place cross. From 1938 to 1950 the owner ran a club where, he said, 'black and white worked together behind the footlights and sat together out front.' New York Confidential called it one of the most famed cabarets in the Village, New York's neighborhood for 'long-haired men, short-haired women, and those not sure exactly what they are' — and noted with alarm that the club's patrons 'hopped across the race fence.'

beats.script_body: Over the years Café Society hosted jazz greats including Billie Holiday, Lena Horne, Sarah Vaughan, and Art Tatum. Its patrons included prominent figures in lesbian and gay history and in the history of the American left, among them Eleanor Roosevelt; Lillian Hellman, sometime Village resident and author of the lesbian-themed drama The Children's Hour; and Paul Robeson.

beats.script_body: In the late 1930s a young man named Bayard Rustin frequented Café Society as both patron and performer — an aspiring singer attending City College who would become a key figure in the Civil Rights movement. A committed disciple of nonviolence, Rustin went to prison as a conscientious objector during World War II and served as an important lieutenant of A. Philip Randolph in the 1940s, until an arrest in California for soliciting another man for sex forced him to take a lower profile. During the Montgomery bus boycott he went south and worked with King behind the scenes, helping make nonviolence King's strategic focus, and remained one of King's closest advisers until the early 1960s — when a rival civil rights leader threatened to spread the false rumor that King and Rustin were having an affair, and King distanced himself to avert a scandal. In 1963 Randolph brought Rustin back as his deputy for planning the March on Washington. Despite Strom Thurmond denouncing him from the Senate floor as a pervert and a Communist, the march was a triumph. Those in the know called Rustin 'Mr. March,' but he never received the public credit he deserved before his death in 1987.

beats.source_passage: In the late 1930s, a young man named Bayard Rustin frequented Café Society both as patron and performer. An aspiring singer who was attending City College at the time, Rustin would go on to become a key figure in the Civil Rights movement. Rustin was a committed disciple of nonviolence who went to prison as a conscientious objector during World War II. He was an important lieutenant of A. Philip Randolph during the 1940s, before an arrest in California for soliciting another man for sex forced him to take a lower profile in organizing efforts. During the Montgomery bus boycott, Rustin went south and worked with King behind the scenes, helping him make nonviolence his strategic focus. Rustin was one of King's closest advisers until the early 1960s, when a rival civil rights leader threatened to spread the false rumor that King and Rustin were having an affair. To avert a scandal, King distanced himself from Rustin. In 1963, A. Philip Randolph brought Rustin back into the fold, making him his deputy for the planning of the March on Washington. Despite attacks by Strom Thurmond, who denounced Rustin from the floor of the Senate as a pervert and a Communist, the march was a success. Those in the know called Rustin "Mr. March," but he never received the public credit he deserved before his death in 1987.

beats.script_body: No. 337 Bleecker Street was the former home of Lorraine Hansberry, the African American playwright whose A Raisin in the Sun brought a groundbreaking portrayal of black family life to Broadway when it opened in 1959. The play ran for two years, and Hansberry became the first black playwright to win the New York Drama Critics Circle Award for Best Play of the Year. Married to Robert Nemiroff, she wrote anonymous letters during the 1950s to One magazine and The Ladder, early gay-rights publications; Nemiroff was aware of her lesbianism, and the couple divorced in 1964 but remained close.

beats.source_passage: Return to Seventh Avenue South and, crossing the avenue, walk west on Christopher Street one block and then turn right on Bleecker, going a few buildings to No. 337, the former home of Lorraine Hansberry. Lorraine Hansberry was an African American playwright whose A Raisin in the Sun brought a groundbreaking portrayal of black family life to Broadway when it opened in 1959. The play ran for two years, and Hansberry became the first black playwright to win the New York Drama Critics Circle Award for Best Play of the Year. Hansberry was married to Robert Nemiroff, but during the 1950s, she wrote a number of anonymous letters to One magazine and The Ladder, publications of "homophile organizations" that were just beginning to campaign for gay rights. Nemiroff was aware of her lesbianism. The couple divorced in 1964 but remained close.

beats.script_body: Bleecker Street was notorious in the mid- to late nineteenth century, second only to the Bowery for its rough and racy reputation, and Greene and Mercer Streets were among the busiest red-light districts in the city. In the early 1890s, in the building that now houses Kenny's Castaways at 157 Bleecker Street, an entrepreneur opened a drag club called the Slide. Such clubs — the most famous being Columbia Hall, a.k.a. 'Paresis Hall,' at 392 Bowery — were places where straight patrons came to gape, but also centers of gay male social life and relatively safe gathering places. The Slide quickly became infamous: in 1892 the New York Herald reported that out-of-towners seeking 'the low life' were directed there first by detectives. A vice cop described the waiters as 'men of degenerate type,' some 'rouging their necks,' who in falsetto voices 'sang filthy ditties' and dropped into a chair at any visitor's table. The police closed the Slide in 1892. Down the block at 183 Bleecker Street, a sex club called the Black Rabbit featuring gay-themed acts managed to stay open until a police raid in 1900.

beats.source_passage: Bleecker Street was notorious in the mid– to late nineteenth century, second only to the Bowery in its reputation as a rough and racy part of town. Greene and Mercer Streets were among the busiest red-light districts in the city. In the early 1890s, in the building that now houses Kenny's Castaways, an entrepreneur started a drag club called the Slide. The most famous was Columbia Hall (a.k.a. "Paresis Hall," after a kind of madness that comes from syphilis) at 392 Bowery. The Slide quickly became infamous. In 1892, the New York Herald reported that the Slide was becoming a tourist attraction for out-of-towners seeking a glimpse of the low life in the city. The Slide was closed by the police in 1892. (Down the block at 183 Bleecker Street, a sex club called the Black Rabbit, featuring gay-themed acts, managed to stay open until 1900, when it, too, was raided by the police.)

beats.script_body: Across the street from the Slide is an apartment building now called the Atrium. Above the modern lettering you can still see the shadow of its old name, 'Mills House No. 1.' The Mills Houses were male residence halls created by philanthropist Darius O. Mills to provide sanitary and moral accommodation for unmarried working men; this one was built in 1896. As historian George Chauncey notes, these inexpensive rooms were home to a number of working-class gay men, including a few who ended up in court for homosexual activity.

beats.script_body: By the late 1800s, the streets of the Village south of West Fourth Street and Washington Square Park had become the city's second most important Little Italy. Greenwich House at 27 Barrow Street, a settlement house founded by Mary Simkovitch in 1904, is a reminder of that past. It offered English classes, cooking lessons for immigrant women coping with unfamiliar American ingredients, and activities for neighborhood children. Further evidence of the former Italian presence survives along Bleecker and Cornelia Streets, where Italian businesses and restaurants remain.

beats.source_passage: By the late 1800s, the streets of the Village south of West Fourth Street and Washington Square Park had become the city's second most important Little Italy. The settlement house provided classes in English for members of the community, cooking lessons for immigrant women dealing with unfamiliar American ingredients, and activities for the neighborhood's children when they weren't in school. beats.script_body: Until the Civil War, the southeastern section of Greenwich Village was home to one of New York's largest African American communities, an area known as 'Little Africa,' and many buildings along Minetta Lane and Minetta Street survive from that period. Among Little Africa's residents in the 1860s was Addie Brown, a young black woman from Connecticut who worked as a domestic servant. From her room in the Sullivan Street house of her employer, a prosperous African American man named John H. Jackson, Brown wrote letters to her dearest love, Rebecca Primus, a black woman from Hartford with whom she had an intimate 'romantic friendship.' Their correspondence is one of the most remarkable surviving documents of romantic friendship between women from the nineteenth century — and one of the few examples of black women's writing from the mid-1800s. The record is uneven: 120 of Brown's letters survive, but none of Primus's replies. In 1859 Brown wrote, 'How did I miss you last night. I did not have anyone to hug me up and to kiss. No kisses is like yours.' Primus's family knew of the bond; in 1866, after a gentleman caller disparaged their affection, Mrs. Primus said that if either woman were a gentleman they would marry. Both women eventually married men, though their letters reveal ambivalence and tension about those decisions.

beats.source_passage: Until the time of the Civil War, the southeastern section of Greenwich Village was home to one of New York City's largest African American communities, in an area known as "Little Africa." Many of the buildings along Minetta Lane and Minetta Street survive from that period. Among Little Africa's many residents in the 1860s was a young black woman from Connecticut named Addie Brown, who worked as a domestic servant. One of her employers, a prosperous African American man named John H. Jackson, had a house on Sullivan Street and ran a hotel on Broadway. From her room in Jackson's house, Brown wrote letters to her dearest love, Rebecca Primus, a black woman from Hartford with whom she had an intimate and passionate "romantic friendship." 120 of Brown's letters to Primus have survived, but none of Primus's replies. In 1859, Brown wrote to Primus: "How did I miss you last night. I did not have anyone to hug me up and to kiss. No kisses is like yours." In 1866, Brown visited Primus's family... Mrs. Primus defended them... "She also said if either one of us was a gent we would marry." Both Primus and Brown eventually married men, though the letters reveal ambivalence and tension about their decisions.

beats.script_body: Eve Addams's Tea Room at 129 MacDougal Street was New York City's first lesbian bar. 'Eve Addams' was Eva Kochever, a Polish Jewish immigrant who opened her business here in 1925, hanging a sign outside the door that read 'Men admitted but not welcome.' In 1926 police raided the bar and charged Kochever with writing an obscene book and with disorderly conduct. After serving a one-year sentence in a New York prison, she was deported to Paris in December 1927.

beats.script_body: At 146 MacDougal stood the Calypso Restaurant, where James Baldwin worked as a waiter in the early 1940s. The gay African American writer befriended many locals who came to see him there, including Henry Miller, Paul Robeson, Marlon Brando, and Eartha Kitt. Baldwin met Brando — who lived nearby on Patchin Place and never tried to hide his own homosexual impulses — when the two were students at the New School. In 1956 Baldwin would publish Giovanni's Room, his second novel and one of the first to deal openly and centrally with homosexuality.

beats.script_body: New Bohemia's artists even witnessed periods of 'lesbian chic.' In a famous tale from the 1920s, poet Edna St. Vincent Millay, seeking relief from persistent headaches, asked an analyst's advice at a party. The analyst, not wanting to shock her, gently suggested she might have 'an occasional impulse towards a person of your own sex.' Millay shot back: 'Oh, you mean I'm a homosexual! Of course I am, and heterosexual too, but what's that got to do with my headache?'

beats.source_passage: This community was tolerant of homosexuality in its ranks and even witnessed periods of what might be termed "lesbian chic." In a famous tale from the 1920s, poet Edna St. Vincent Millay conveys the spirit of the times in her exchange with an analyst. Seeking relief from persistent headaches, Millay asked an analyst's advice at a party. The analyst, not wanting to shock this lovely woman, said: "I wonder if it has ever occurred to you that you might perhaps... have an occasional impulse towards a person of your own sex?" Millay responded: "Oh, you mean I'm a homosexual! Of course I am, and heterosexual too, but what's that got to do with my headache?"

beats.script_body: From about 1908 to 1913, 82 Washington Place was home to novelist Willa Cather and her partner Edith Lewis. Cather — author of My Ántonia and Death Comes for the Archbishop — had two central relationships with other women and referred to herself as 'William' in letters to a woman she admired as an undergraduate at the University of Nebraska. Cather and Lewis lived together at various Greenwich Village addresses for nearly forty years, until Cather's death in 1947. She took great care to destroy most of her personal correspondence before she died, and in one surviving college letter she laments her 'unnatural' attraction to another woman.

beats.script_body: As you walk through Washington Square Park, you're passing over the remains of probably thousands of bodies interred here during its years as a potter's field in the eighteenth century. A yellow fever epidemic in 1822 forced many to flee downtown for the 'village,' and many stayed as the area developed; luxury townhouses appeared on the park's northern edge in the 1830s. The Arch itself was designed by Stanford White in 1892 to replace a papier-mâché antecedent erected in 1889 to celebrate the centennial of George Washington's return to the city after the Revolutionary War.

A yellow fever epidemic in 1822 forced many to flee downtown New York City for the "village." In the 1830s, luxury townhouses appeared on the northern edge of the park and some still remain. beats.script_body: In her apartment at 23 Fifth Avenue, Mabel Dodge ran a weekly salon that became a center for Village artists and intellectuals. Openly bisexual, Dodge opened her doors to many unconventional women, including Emma Goldman, Margaret Sanger, and Gertrude Stein — whose work A Portrait of Mabel Dodge was named in the hostess's honor. Dodge was also one of the people who made possible the Armory Art Show, which opened in February 1913, bringing Marcel Duchamp's Nude Descending a Staircase and works by Picasso and Cézanne to the protesting masses.

beats.script_body: 86 University Place was the former site of the Bagatelle, one of the few lesbian bars in the city in the 1950s, alongside the more working-class Sea Colony and the Swing Rendezvous. Black poet and essayist Audre Lorde wrote about the Bagatelle in her autobiography Zami: A New Spelling of My Name. There was a tiny dance floor in back, and the front room 'smelled like plastic and blue glass and beer and lots of good-looking young women.' Lorde recalled that she and the other 'out' black lesbians rarely acknowledged one another, and that 'the Bag was always The Club.'

beats.source_passage: Walk east to University Place and then north to 86 University Place, the former site of the Bagatelle. The Bagatelle was one of the few lesbian bars in the city in the 1950s. The other popular ones were the Sea Colony (a more working-class bar on Eighth Avenue) and the Swing Rendezvous (on MacDougal Street). Audre Lorde, black poet and essayist, wrote about spending time at the Bagatelle in her autobiography Zami: A New Spelling of My Name. There was a tiny dance floor in the back, and the front room "smelled like plastic and blue glass and beer and lots of good-looking young women." While there were other places for women to go at the time, she said that "the Bag was always The Club."

beats.script_body: From 1913 through the 1930s, Webster Hall at 125 East Eleventh Street hosted the annual Greenwich Village Ball — masquerade balls patronized by the Village's bohemian society, including many gay men in drag. By the early 1920s, gay men and lesbians held events of their own there. In 1934 the New York Herald Tribune described the scene: 'Men danced with women in men's clothes. Women danced with men in women's clothes. And strange androgynous couples careened about the floor, oblivious to the workings of society and nature.' Today Webster Hall is a popular, mostly straight nightclub.

beats.script_body: The drag balls gave rise to one of gay life's most familiar terms: coming out. Today it suggests emerging from the closet, but its earlier ball-scene origins were lighter — participants used 'coming out' with a wink toward straight debutantes. As the Baltimore Afro-American put it in 1931, the 'coming out of new debutantes into homosexual society' was the outstanding feature of Baltimore's eighth annual 'pansy' ball.

beats.source_passage: The drag balls gave rise to the use of one of contemporary gay life's most familiar terms: coming out. Today, coming out is generally thought of as "coming out of the closet," emerging from terrified secrecy. Earlier origins of the phrase in the ball scene, however, were much less dark and sad. Participants in the balls used the term coming out with a wink and a nod to straight debutantes. As the Baltimore Afro-American put it in 1931: "Debutantes Bow at Local 'Pansy' Ball: The coming out of new debutantes into homosexual society was the outstanding feature of Baltimore's eighth annual frolic of the pansies..."

beats.script_body: The house at 457 Sixth Avenue was the former home of Murray Hall, a 'ward heeler' for Tammany Hall who organized the vote in this district. Married twice and known as a heavy drinker, a brawler, and 'sweet on women,' Hall died in 1901 leaving a wife and an adopted daughter — and the revelation that Hall had died of breast cancer and had been a woman who passed as a man for all of her adult life. The New York Times covered the story for days. One lawyer friend insisted, 'I saw him play poker like a veteran... I just can't believe he was a woman, that's all,' still referring to Hall as 'he.'

beats.script_body: From the 1920s through the 1950s, 171 West Twelfth Street was home to a network of lesbian couples and comrades-in-arms: artist Nancy Cook and educator Marion Dickerman; activist Polly Porter and Democratic official Molly Dewson; and Grace Hutchins and Anna Rochester, both Communist Party leaders. Many — especially Dickerman and Cook — were good friends with Eleanor Roosevelt, who kept her own apartments at 20 East Eleventh Street and later at 29 Washington Square West. When Franklin D. Roosevelt became president, Eleanor became a fierce champion for women in government, and many of her friends gained New Deal posts: Molly Dewson directed the Women's Division of the Democratic National Committee, and among the president's appointees were Frances Perkins, the first woman cabinet member, and Grace Abbott of the Children's Bureau. Roosevelt herself had an intimate relationship with Associated Press reporter Lorena Hickok, assigned in 1932 to cover the new first lady; their letters reveal a passionate intimacy, though many biographers strenuously insist Roosevelt was not a lesbian.

beats.script_body: Since 1984, 208 West Thirteenth Street has been the home base for New York's gay and lesbian community. The Lesbian and Gay Community Services Center hosts dozens of meetings and events on any given day, with rooms for numerous LGBT organizations. On March 14, 1987, novelist and activist Larry Kramer — scheduled to read from one of his novels — instead rose and delivered an impassioned plea for action on AIDS. Within a week, the AIDS Coalition to Unleash Power, or ACT UP, was founded, rejuvenating gay and lesbian activism in the Reagan era and forcing action on AIDS by pharmaceutical companies and governments.

beats.script_body: Julius', at 159 West Tenth Street, dates back to before Prohibition and is one of the oldest bars still open in the Village — and the site of an important early gay rights victory in New York State. In 1966 the Mattachine Society of New York staged what it called a 'sip-in,' consciously borrowing from the civil rights movement. At the time, if a bartender knowingly served alcohol to a homosexual, the State Liquor Authority could rescind the bar's license, and bars around the Village posted signs reading 'If you're gay, go away.' Members went from bar to bar, sat down, announced they were homosexual, and ordered drinks. In most places they were served — but at Julius' they were refused. Working with the City Human Rights Commission, the Mattachine Society sued, and in 1967 the New York State Supreme Court ruled that the liquor authority needed substantial evidence of indecent behavior — not just same-sex kissing or touching — to close a bar. That precedent would matter just two years later and two blocks away.

beats.script_body: This stretch of Christopher Street is widely considered the birthplace of the modern lesbian and gay rights movement. The bar that once stood here at No. 53, the Stonewall Inn, was an unprepossessing place — crowded and popular on weekends but nothing fancy. Like most bars serving a gay clientele, it was owned by the Mob, which paid off the local police; raids and shakedowns were the norm, and many such bars had a light over the door that flashed when the police were coming. In the early morning hours of June 28, 1969, the patrons fought back. When the cops singled out several drag queens for arrest and pushed the rest into the street, refusing to disperse, one butch lesbian struck the officer who had hit her, and the crowd unleashed a hail of coins and invective. The police were forced back into the bar; the crowd attacked the building and tried to set it on fire, leading the cops to draw their guns. Riot police averted a possible shooting, but the crowd would not back down. Those actions sparked several nights of unrest and launched a new phase of activism — 'gay liberation.'

disputes.external_finding: Sources (Wikipedia, Village Preservation) state Stonewall was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on June 28, 1999, and elevated to National Historic Landmark status the following year (2000, late Clinton administration). The book conflates the 1999 NRHP listing with NHL status. Both agree 1999 was the first federal LGBT-history recognition.

beats.script_body: On the first anniversary of the riots, New York witnessed its first Gay Pride march, up Sixth Avenue from Christopher Street to Central Park; every year since, the riots have been remembered worldwide with June parades. As one activist quipped, 'I am probably one of six people who lived in the Village at the time who does not claim to have been at the Stonewall riots.' The riots spurred two organizations: the Gay Liberation Front, launched immediately after, and the Gay Activists Alliance, which split off in December 1969 after infighting over the scope of the work. The GLF saw itself as part of the New Left and pushed coalition politics; the GAA had a constitution barring alliance with any organization not directly related to the homosexual cause. Together they answered homophobia with 'zap' actions and created new visibility. The first GLF meetings were held at an organization called Alternate U at 534 Sixth Avenue, and from 1971 to 1974 the GAA was headquartered in a renovated firehouse at 99 Wooster Street — the GAA Firehouse, a center of gay life until it was firebombed in October 1974 amid a rash of arson attacks on gay bars, homes, and offices.

The GAA Firehouse became a center of gay life and activism until it was firebombed in October 1974.

beats.script_body: The 'love that dare not speak its name' has in fact had many names. In the 1860s a gay German writer and activist, Karl Heinrich Ulrichs, coined 'Uranians' — people physically male or female but with the spirit of the opposite sex — drawing the term from Plato's Symposium to create a respectable label, rejecting 'pervert' and 'sodomite.' The word homosexual first appeared in an 1868 letter to Ulrichs. On the New York streets, 'fairy' was the common word for an effeminate gay man, with 'queer' as the more universal term; black gay men and lesbians spoke of being 'in the life.' The word gay itself first meant prostitutes — 'gay women' — and was adopted as a code word that police did not crack until the late 1940s.

beats.script_body: The Daughters of Bilitis, founded in San Francisco in 1955, was part of the first wave of the organized gay rights movement and published a magazine called The Ladder from 1956 to 1970. Its first New York chapter was organized in 1958 by activist Barbara Gittings and from 1963 ran out of a basement office at 26-32 Charlton Street. The chapter was at the forefront of public actions, including the 'Annual Reminder' marches at Independence Hall in Philadelphia from 1963 to 1969 and a 1965 picket at the White House protesting the ban on gay federal employees. The DOB was one of the 'homophile' organizations of the 1950s — alongside the Mattachine Society (1950) and ONE (1954) — which took a conservative approach, asking members to 'dress appropriately,' men in suits and women in skirts.

beats.script_body: In 1777 a man wrote to another man: 'I wish, my dear Laurens, it might be in my power, by action rather than words, to convince you that I love you.' The writer was Alexander Hamilton, addressing a fellow soldier in the Continental Army. Historians have long debated such effusive correspondence between people of the same sex from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries — what they call 'romantic friendships' in an intensely homosocial age. Among those whose letters reveal such attachments are Ralph Waldo Emerson, Margaret Fuller, and Susan B. Anthony. By the late 1800s, women's long-term partnerships came to be known as 'Boston marriages,' a term drawn from Henry James's novel The Bostonians.

Emerson, Margaret Fuller, and Susan B. Anthony wrote such letters

review_queue.description: Greenwich House: book says 'founded by Mary Simkovitch in 1904'; consensus sources say Greenwich House was founded/incorporated in 1902 by Mary Kingsbury Simkhovitch, with the 27 Barrow Street building opening in 1917. Book's date (1904) and name spelling ('Simkovitch') both differ.
review_queue.recommendation: Keep the beat with fact_check_status='disputed'. Do NOT auto-correct — founding-date nuance; the book may mark a later milestone. Consider footnoting the 1902 founding / 1917 building dates at upload.

review_queue.description: Café Society: book says it ran '1938 to 1950'; most sources give the downtown Sheridan Square club as 1938–1948, with final sale of both clubs by 1950.
review_queue.recommendation: Leave book value; the 1950 endpoint is defensible (sale). Not auto-corrected.

review_queue.description: Stonewall: book says the blocks were 'designated a National Historic Landmark' in 1999; sources show 1999 = National Register listing, with NHL status in 2000. The book's headline claim (1999, first federal LGBT-history recognition) is accurate; only the NRHP-vs-NHL label is off by a year.
review_queue.recommendation: Leave as a minor dispute note; core fact verified. Not auto-corrected.
